title: Structural and functional characterization of polyclonal antibody responses reveals shared and distinct antigenic features of RSV and hMPV fusion proteins
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV), members of the Pneumoviridae family, circulate widely and are leading causes of hospitalization for acute respiratory infections in infants and older adults. The viral fusion (F) protein in its prefusion (preF) conformation is the primary target of neutralizing antibodies, yet how naturally elicited circulating polyclonal antibodies are distributed across its antigenic landscape remains poorly understood. Here, we combined serological profiling, site-specific antibody competition assays and electron microscopy-based polyclonal epitope mapping (EMPEM) to characterize preF-directed immunity to RSV and hMPV in healthy adults. All donors exhibited detectable preF-binding antibodies that positively correlated with virus neutralization and broadly recognized multiple antigenic sites, consistent with immunodominance patterns predicted by a surface-centric computational model. Despite this overall similarity, the distribution of responses across individual antigenic sites differed between RSV and hMPV. EMPEM analyses revealed consistent targeting of the highly neutralization-sensitive preF apex (site Ø) in both viruses, alongside less abundant responses against equatorial and upper-middle epitopes (sites II, III, IV and V). We additionally observed antibody-bound destabilized preF, supporting a model in which antibody binding promotes transient opening of the preF trimer and may interfere with the conformational rearrangements required for membrane fusion. Together, these findings highlight apex-directed antibodies as a prominent feature of naturally acquired pneumovirus immunity in adults and reveal both shared and distinct patterns of antigenic recognition that may inform next-generation vaccine design and antibody-based prophylactics.

title: Stroke Triggered by Respiratory Viruses: Ecological Study of Temporal and Spatiotemporal Associations
abstract: BACKGROUND: Infections have been linked as short-term triggers for stroke, but the extent of their contribution is unclear. We examined population-level temporal and spatiotemporal associations between common respiratory viruses and stroke in an ecological study in Victoria, Australia. METHODS: The statewide Victorian Admitted Episodes data set, covering all hospital admissions for stroke between June 2010 and December 2022, was analyzed against statewide representative data from SnotWatch respiratory polymerase chain reaction tests. Population size, climate, and air pollution data sets for the same period were treated as population-level confounders. Time-series analysis was used to model weekly stroke events and respiratory virus levels (% of polymerase chain reaction tests positive for each pathogen), and attributable fractions were computed using distributed lag nonlinear modeling. To examine spatiotemporal variation, the weekly association by Statistical Area Level 2 was modeled using a Bayesian Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. RESULTS: We analyzed 153 730 stroke events (61% ischemic, 25% hemorrhagic, and 14% unspecified) and 6 180 896 respiratory specimens. In the time-series analysis, higher weekly levels of specific respiratory viruses were associated with increased rates of stroke after controlling for confounders. Our model estimated that the fractions of strokes attributed to enterovirus and human metapneumovirus 4.6% (95% CI, 2.5-6.6) and 1.3% (95% CI, 0.3-2.3), respectively, which rose during peak viral weeks. The attributable fractions differed between ischemic stroke (human metapneumovirus 3.7%) and hemorrhagic stroke (enterovirus, 5.8%; parainfluenza, 3.2%). Spatiotemporal analysis revealed greater effect sizes in areas potentially associated with agricultural/industrial activity, as well as in outer-urban areas, based on the regionality of the Statistical Area Level 2 of usual patient residence. CONCLUSIONS: At the population level, there were clear, observable time- and space-time-related associations between respiratory virus activity and stroke. People living in higher-risk areas during peak respiratory virus periods may be more susceptible to acute stroke. This warrants further investigation.

title: Decision-Making About Respiratory Syncytial Virus Immunization for Infants: Qualitative Interview Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the United States. Although maternal RSV vaccination and infant RSV monoclonal antibody products are recommended to protect infants during their first RSV season, uptake has remained modest. Understanding how pregnant individuals make decisions about these products is critical for informing strategies that support timely immunization. OBJECTIVE: The study aimed to examine the behavioral and social drivers shaping decisions regarding RSV vaccination during pregnancy and infant RSV monoclonal antibody immunization among pregnant individuals in the United States. METHODS: We conducted an exploratory qualitative study from a relativist epistemological perspective, using semistructured interviews with 12 pregnant and postpartum adults recruited across the United States between October 2024 and May 2025. Participants were purposively sampled to include individuals with positive, uncertain, and negative intentions toward RSV vaccination. Interviews were guided by the World Health Organization's behavioral and social drivers of vaccination framework and analyzed using a framework analysis approach. Screening survey data were summarized descriptively to characterize participant immunization intentions and contextualize the qualitative findings. RESULTS: RSV immunization decisions reflected interacting behavioral, emotional, social, and practical influences rather than attitudes alone. Participants with positive vaccination intentions described greater trust in medical expertise, confidence in vaccination, and personal or professional experience with RSV illness. Those with unsure or negative intentions emphasized the novelty of RSV vaccines, concerns about safety and long-term effects, and greater reliance on clinician recommendations and peer experiences when making decisions. Across intention groups, participants expressed a preference for receiving protection during pregnancy rather than after birth but reported uncertainty related to vaccine availability, timing within the 32- to 36-week eligibility window, and inconsistent integration into prenatal care. Participants consistently identified trusted clinician communication, opportunities for early discussion, and access to clear educational materials as important influences on decision-making. CONCLUSIONS: Decisions regarding RSV immunization during pregnancy are shaped by interconnected motivational, interpersonal, and structural factors. Integrating education on RSV and RSV immunization options earlier in prenatal care, strengthening clinician recommendations, and reducing logistical barriers to maternal vaccination may improve informed decision-making and timely uptake of infant RSV protection.

title: Risk factors and aetiological agents of community-acquired pneumonia in children under five years in South Asia: A systematic review
abstract: Pneumonia remains a leading cause of mortality among children under five years in South Asia, a region that, with sub-Saharan Africa, accounts for over half of the world's childhood pneumonia cases. To our knowledge, no prior review has jointly synthesised the risk factors and aetiological agents of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in under-fives specific to this region. This systematic review aimed to identify, critically appraise, and synthesise available evidence on the risk factors and aetiological agents associated with CAP in children under five years of age in South Asian countries. Following PRISMA guidelines, four electronic databases (MEDLINE, PubMed, Global Health, and Web of Science) were systematically searched for studies published between January 2000 and July 2024, with the search updated to January 2026. Quality assessment was performed using the Crowe Critical Appraisal Tool (CCAT), with only high-quality studies (≥75% score) included in the final synthesis. Data were synthesised narratively due to heterogeneity in study designs and outcome measures. From 1196 records identified and 747 studies screened, 16 met the inclusion criteria after quality assessment (8 on risk factors, 8 on aetiology), conducted across five South Asian countries (India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, Bhutan). Young age (children 0–23 months), malnutrition (particularly underweight and wasting), and incomplete immunisation emerged as the most consistently identified risk factors across studies. Environmental exposures, including indoor air pollution, poor ventilation, and overcrowding, were significant contributors. Viral pathogens predominated in aetiological studies, with respiratory syncytial virus being the most frequently identified pathogen (mean detection rate 29.2%). Blood culture positivity for bacterial pathogens was generally lower (1.5-31.3%; below 13% in four of five studies), with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus most common among positive cultures. This systematic review demonstrates that childhood CAP in South Asia results from a complex interplay of modifiable host, environmental, and socioeconomic risk factors. Integrated interventions addressing nutrition, immunization coverage, household air pollution, and socioeconomic determinants are essential for reducing the substantial pneumonia burden among South Asian children.

full_text: Abstract Purpose To compare the prevalence, microbiological characteristics, and clinical impact of bacterial co-infection in adults hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) or influenza A infection. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed RSV or influenza A infection in Central Denmark. Bacterial co-infection was identified using bacterial culturing and urinary antigen testing. Poisson regression was used to estimate risk ratios for bacterial co-infection, and Cox proportional hazards regression was used to evaluate associations between bacterial co-infection and adverse clinical outcomes. Results Among 4,537 patients, 1,394 had RSV infection and 3,143 had influenza A infection. Among patients undergoing microbiological testing, bacterial co-infection was identified in 187/611 (30.6%) RSV-infected patients and 298/947 (31.5%) influenza A-infected patients (p = 0.72). Among all patients bacterial co-infection was identified in 187/1,394 (13.4%) RSV infected patients and 298/3,143 (9.5%) influenza A infected patients (p < 0.01) Haemophilus influenzae was the most common pathogen in both groups, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis and Staphylococcus aureus. Bacterial co-infection was associated with increased ICU admission and mortality among influenza A infected patients, whereas estimates were lower in RSV. Conclusions Among patients undergoing microbiological testing, bacterial co-infection was identified at similar rates in patients hospitalized with RSV and influenza A infection. The most frequently isolated bacteria in both viral groups were bacterial species harboring genes for beta-lactamase production. These findings support consideration of tailoring the empirical antibiotic therapy to cover pathogens with beta-lactamase production when bacterial co-infection is suspected in RSV and influenza A infected patients. Bacterial co-infection was associated with poorer clinical outcomes in Influenza A than RSV.
